source_title: HPE NVIDIA L20 specifications; enterprise 2U GPU-server engineering envelope
notes: Each L20 board is specified at ~300-350 W depending OEM document. Two GPUs alone are 0.6-0.7 kW; host CPUs, memory, disks and fans add substantial power. This is wall-power envelope, not GPU TDP sum.

source_title: NVIDIA DCGM L20 idle observation; enterprise-server idle evidence
notes: A reported L20 idled near 36 W; two idle GPUs therefore contribute only ~0.07 kW. Remaining host, memory, fans, NICs and PSU losses dominate. The old 0.42 kW assumption is plausible for an online-idle server, not for a powered-off spare.

source_title: NVIDIA DCGM issue showing L20 power reading
notes: Observed power draw 36.13 W on an L20 in DCGM output. Configuration-specific; use only as a GPU-idle anchor.

source_title: vLLM Sleep Mode; L20 idle observation
notes: vLLM sleep frees/offloads model resources but does not power off the host. Energy benefit is mainly avoiding active GPU/model work; host idle remains.

source_title: ENERGY STAR server/BMC off-mode guidance; enterprise BMC architecture
notes: Modern BMC/PSU standby draw varies. Use 20 W base rather than hundreds of watts for a cold spare that remains remotely manageable.

source_title: HPE Gen11 cold-boot expectations and enterprise server POST evidence
notes: Enterprise POST and hardware initialization are measured in minutes, unlike commodity PCs. Exact WR5220 boot time should be measured.

source_title: vLLM cold-start characterization; Tensorfuse optimization example
notes: Typical components include model load, GPU transfer, compile, CUDA graph capture and NCCL. Fresh starts can take tens of seconds to several minutes.

source_title: Combined enterprise boot + vLLM cold start
notes: Use as startup-delay parameter if cold spares can be activated. Base 7 min is deliberately conservative.

source_title: Operational engineering assumption
notes: Avoid cycling servers for short valleys and model-loading overhead. Not a hardware minimum; a scheduling regularization parameter.

source_title: No robust evidence for material wear cost at hourly cycling
notes: For a 24h prototype, model startup delay/minimum-on-time rather than a monetary startup cost. A tiny penalty can prevent chattering.

source_title: Engineering practice assumption
notes: The core planning headroom is 15% above average required compute capacity. Sensitivity cases are 0%, 15%, 30%, and 50%. This headroom and any separate N+1 discreteness are engineering scenarios, not an observed manufacturing-sector average. Normal operation may use 100% of installed capacity.

source_title: Cold-start evidence + enterprise SLA logic
notes: If 5-15 minute recovery is acceptable, most N+1 spare capacity need not remain OS-on. Critical low-latency HA may instead require a hot replica.

source_title: Enterprise availability engineering
notes: Base keeps one server warm for interactive traffic. High case keeps two for immediate failover/model isolation.

source_title: Cloud elasticity model
notes: Customer generally does not purchase a permanently idle physical spare; reserve is supplied by provider pooling. Optional 5% covers application-level headroom.

source_title: Capacity-planning engineering assumption
notes: Use only for social resource-cost scenarios, not the enterprise cloud bill. Provider-specific fleet reserve/utilization is commercially confidential.
